description: Hey, I’m Surya! I work with Python, ML, CAD/3D engineering, and simulations, and I love building real, working space tools. I’m planning to tackle Lunar Landing Site Navigator and I’ll handle the engineering, NASA data processing, and backend logic. Looking for 1–2 teammates into frontend/UI, 3D/data viz, or video/storytelling so we can ship a standout working prototype in 39 hours. Feel free to reach out!
summary:
I developed Space Conqueror, an interactive 3D lunar mission navigator engineered to evaluate Artemis candidate landing sites at the Moon’s South Pole.

Addressing the challenge of extreme polar topography and permanently shadowed terrain, I synthesized authentic NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA) elevation datasets into a real-time WebGL mission cockpit. Working with Google Antigravity as an engineering partner, I built the platform using React, TypeScript, and Three.js to simulate low-angle solar illumination, dynamic slope hazard heatmaps, and traversability. High-fidelity Artemis lander and rover assemblies were modeled with aerospace precision in CATIA V5 and SolidWorks, textured with photorealistic lunar regolith materials in Blender, and integrated with ground-contact physics.

This tool is critical because Artemis missions require finding landing corridors that balance continuous solar energy, Earth line-of-sight communications, and safe slope gradients. Space Conqueror bridges raw planetary science and accessible simulation, empowering engineers and planners to de-risk surface operations before touchdown.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

I built Space Conqueror as an interactive, browser-based 3D mission cockpit designed to evaluate and navigate Artemis landing zones across the Moon’s South Pole.

The application works by taking raw planetary data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)—specifically the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) 240-meter-per-pixel digital elevation models—and converting that data into true-to-scale 3D terrain meshes. Across six key Artemis candidate landing sites (Shackleton Rim, Malapert Massif, Connecting Ridge, Mons Mouton, Nobile, and Haworth), the cockpit simulates:

  1. Low-Angle Polar Lighting: Because the Sun sits barely above the lunar horizon at the poles, mountains cast long, pitch-black shadows across crater floors. Space Conqueror dynamically calculates solar angles to show shifting shadow boundaries in real time.
  2. Slope Hazard Heatmaps: The system computes analytical surface gradients across every meter of the terrain, dynamically painting slopes green (<10∘<10^\circ<10∘), yellow (10∘–15∘10^\circ–15^\circ10∘–15∘), or red (>15∘>15^\circ>15∘) so landing planners can immediately spot rollover hazards.
  3. Interactive Surface Operations: Users can zoom from orbit down to ground level to inspect a CAD-engineered Artemis Lander touching down on real lunar dirt, deploy a cargo ramp, and drive a compliant-wheeled Lunar Rover across the crater rims using real-time terrain raycasting and suspension physics.

What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Install, Universal Access: Planetary scientists and mission planners typically rely on heavy desktop GIS software (ArcGIS, QGIS, or custom SPICE toolsets) that require high-end workstations and extensive training. Space Conqueror runs entirely in a web browser at 60 FPS on any laptop or phone.
  • Unified Multi-Hazard Visibility: Instead of switching between disconnected 2D maps for elevation, lighting, and communications, Space Conqueror combines solar exposure, slope gradients, and direct-to-Earth visibility into one cohesive visual environment.
  • Ground-Level Operational Testing: You don’t just look at a contour map—you can physically drive a rover across the terrain to test egress routes, identify blind spots behind boulder ridges, and plan traversable corridors before metal touches regolith.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Returning astronauts to the Moon is the most complex spaceflight challenge of this decade. The primary goal of Space Conqueror is to de-risk surface operations at the South Pole. By transforming raw scientific rasters into an intuitive, interactive tool, it helps mission planners, university researchers, and aerospace engineers quickly vet landing sites for solar power stability and terrain navigability.

Beyond engineering, it bridges the gap between deep planetary science and the public. Anyone in the world can open the link, explore the South Pole candidate sites, and understand why landing at the lunar pole is so uniquely challenging and exciting.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Google Antigravity: My autonomous AI engineering partner throughout the challenge. Antigravity helped architect the end-to-end full-stack system, synthesize the Three.js rendering pipelines, automate data transformations, and verify mathematical accuracy.
  • Aerospace CAD (CATIA V5 & SolidWorks): Parametrically designed the mechanical assemblies for the Artemis Lunar Lander (descent frame, ascent stage, engine bell, quad landing gear) and the Lunar Rover (compliant wire-mesh wheels, rocker-bogie chassis, sensor mast) to real aerospace engineering standards.
  • Blender (Python 3D Pipeline): Textured the vehicles with physically based rendering (PBR) regolith materials, modeled realistic lunar optical properties, and baked optimized GLTF/GLB models for low-latency web streaming.
  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) & LOLA: Provided authentic polar elevation rasters (ldem_75s_240m) that form the physical bedrock of the topography.
  • Frontend Cockpit: Built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js / WebGL for in-browser real-time lighting, shadow maps, and ground-contact physics.
  • Scientific Backend: Python & FastAPI, integrating orbital mechanics and ephemeris validation against JPL standards.
  • Deployment & Version Control: Git, GitHub, and Vercel serverless edge hosting.

How is your project creative?

Traditional space mission planning relies on static 2D heatmaps and contour charts. Space Conqueror’s creativity lies in merging aerospace CAD precision with real-time video game mechanics and authentic planetary science.

Instead of reading a report stating that a slope is 16 degrees or that sunlight is lost at 14:00 UTC, the user is immersed directly on the surface: you can watch the Sun dip below the jagged crater rim, cast a 12-kilometer shadow over your solar panels, and test whether your rover can climb out of a permanently shadowed crater trap. It turns dry numbers into a tangible human experience.

What factors did your team consider?

  1. The South Pole’s Extreme Illumination Geometry: The Sun hovers at only 1.5∘1.5^\circ1.5∘ above the horizon. We had to calculate exact solar vectors because a slight dip in terrain can plunge equipment into cryogenic temperatures (40 K40\text{ K}40 K) and complete power loss.
  2. Lander Tip-Over & Rover Rollover Thresholds: Artemis landers cannot safely land on slopes exceeding 12∘–15∘12^\circ–15^\circ12∘–15∘. We prioritized immediate visual gradient detection so unviable zones are immediately flagged.
  3. Direct Line-of-Sight Communications: Lunar mountains easily block direct microwave links back to Earth. We factored in horizon clearance so landing corridors maintain reliable comms links.
  4. Web Optimization & Low-Latency Streaming: Large lunar DEM rasters and complex CAD assemblies can easily freeze a web browser. We implemented dynamic geometric level-of-detail (LOD), binary GLB compression, and asynchronous shader initialization to ensure butter-smooth 60 FPS performance on standard consumer hardware.
